classification.difficultyReason: Separate the inclusive France–Spain count from the triple overlap and choose a workable order for using the three country totals. Then read the exclusive and inclusive events from the completed diagram.

content.prompt: 58 people took a trip to Europe. Each person visited at least one of France, England or Spain. Of this group, 26 visited France, 38 visited England, 29 visited Spain, 10 visited France and Spain, 12 visited only Spain, 13 visited only England and 8 visited all three countries.

spec.sourceRegion: Question 5, three-circle diagram between the givens and the probability prompt
spec.description: Three mutually overlapping unshaded circles in a rectangle, with France above England on the lower left and Spain on the lower right.
spec.mathematics: The figure contains seven distinct regions inside the circles and one outside. Each country name is in its own exclusive region.
spec.answerVisibility: All eight regions have space for handwritten counts. The student figure contains country names only.

children.prompt: A person from the group of 58 was chosen at random. What is the probability that the person visited

answer.short:
$\frac{3}{29}$

Start with the 8 who visited all three countries and fill the pair overlaps before finding the France-only count.
answer.worked:
Place 8 in the centre. France and Spain only has $10-8=2$ people.

England and Spain only has $29-12-2-8=7$ people.

France and England only has $38-13-7-8=10$ people.

France only has $26-10-2-8=6$ people.

$$\begin{align*}P(\text{France only})&=\frac{6}{58}\\P(\text{France only})&=\frac{3}{29}\end{align*}$$

The label is scaled to 84 percent of the standard 10 pt size, in order to retain source placement entirely within the England-only crescent. Keep the count at its regular size below the name.
spec.mathematics: France only 6, England only 13, Spain only 12, France and England only 10, France and Spain only 2, England and Spain only 7, all three 8, outside 0. The counts sum to 58.

answer.worked:
The England–France overlap contains 10 who visited just those two countries and 8 who visited all three. Let $E$ and $F$ be the events of visiting England and France, respectively.

$$\begin{align*}P(E\cap F)&=\frac{10+8}{58}\\P(E\cap F)&=\frac{9}{29}\end{align*}$$

Use the three exclusive regions. Let $A$ be the event of visiting exactly one country.

$$\begin{align*}P(A)&=\frac{6+13+12}{58}\\P(A)&=\frac{31}{58}\end{align*}$$
